name: Lavender violet
lede: Lavender violet is an xkcd survey name that pairs the paler flower color lavender with the stronger, more saturated violet.

sections.title: The flower's name, pushed further
sections.body: The flower lavender, *Lavandula*, gives English its paler, greyer color word of the same name, but this xkcd entry pairs it with *violet* to describe a much stronger, more saturated purple than the flower itself typically shows [1][2]. No source in our library gives a date or author for when volunteers first combined the two words this way beyond the 2010 survey record [1][2]. The 1955 ISCC-NBS system's nearest block, strong purple, sits a wide 12.1 units away, one of the larger gaps, which fits a name built by combining two existing words rather than matching an established standard [2]. In Munsell terms it sits at 0.7P 4.8/18.8, and in LCH at lightness 49, chroma 83, among the most saturated purples in the library, close to [[violet]], [[lilac]] and [[orchid]] [2].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our 23,781-painting archive carries a color within four units of Lavender violet covering at least one per cent of its canvas, as photographed [3]. A purple this saturated is difficult for most historical pigments, including the mineral and lake purples available before synthetic dyes, which tended to be either duller or to fade; it sits closer to a modern dye than to any pigment common in old oil paint [3]. In printed English the two-word phrase rose fastest and peaked around 1910, well before this specific hue was ever recorded [4].

questions.q: Lavender violet is named for a flower, but how does its color differ from the flower's usual pale shade?
choices: It is far more saturated, pushed toward violet
It is a completely different hue
It is identical to the flower
questions.answer: It is far more saturated, pushed toward violet
